extracted.intended_audience: public relations students, educators, and practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook guidance defining public relations as a management function, describing its organizational role, professionalization criteria, use of social science, and four historical/practice models (press agent/publicity, public-information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as management of communication between an organization and its publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is the management of communication between an organization and its publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition emphasizes that PR ‘‘manages the movement of messages into the organization’’ (research on publics to counsel management) and ‘‘out of the organization’’ (help management explain policy or action, prepare news stories, fact sheets). It is offered as the working definition for the book and is deliberately broad to include varying tools and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on management role
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is a management function: plan, manage, and execute communication for the organization as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners may conduct research on knowledge/attitudes/behaviors of publics, counsel management on policy and action, write news stories or fact sheets, manage employee communications, and otherwise serve as part of the management subsystem. Emphasizes two-way communication with both management and external publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization requirements (body of knowledge, technical expertise, ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a true profession PR must possess a body of knowledge, mastered communication techniques, a set of values, and a code of ethics that discourage antisocial uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The profession should professionalize rather than be banned when misused. True professionals have knowledge and skills (similar to law or medicine), plus ethics and responsibility. Anti-patterns: press agentry/propaganda roots, practitioners with little formal training or social-science grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social science / communication research
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should be based on knowledge from the social sciences and communication research (communication science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social sciences include communication science, psychology, economics, sociology, political science, anthropology, geography, etc. Students/practitioners need focused exposure to concepts relevant to PR problems to avoid 'information overload.' Communication research informs research, planning, and evaluation of PR programs, activities, and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of theory and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: PR education/practice should integrate conceptual frameworks from social/behavioral sciences with technical communication skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conceptual framework should help practitioners know when and how to use technical skills, not just teach theory for theory's sake. The book aims to provide both a conceptual framework and a set of technical skills for research, planning, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core functions and desired effects (Harlow's extended definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should: establish and maintain lines of communication, acceptance and cooperation between an organization and its publics; involve management of problems or issues; keep management informed and responsive to public opinion; emphasize responsibility to serve the public interest; help anticipate trends; and use research and sound and ethical communication techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This longer definition enumerates practical aims and tools of PR. Guidance includes that not all practitioners will use all tools or achieve all effects; the definition is intended to include both professional and nonprofessional PR activities and various effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of practice: press agent / publicity model
rubrics_metrics.description: Press agent/publicity model: publicity-driven practice oriented toward promotion and 'spreading the faith'—historically earlier stage of PR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found in earlier stages of history and in some contemporary practice; objectives and settings differ from other models. Typically one-way, promotional, and based on attracting attention rather than mutual adjustment. Evaluation means differ (e.g., media hits, attention) from models focused on mutual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of practice: public-information model
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-information model: deliberate, planned, and sustained effort to establish and maintain mutual understanding primarily by disseminating information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes providing information (often one-way) through media; common in governmental and institutional settings. Objectives and evaluation differ from advocacy or two-way persuasion models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of practice: two-way asymmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-way asymmetric model: uses research and feedback to persuade publics—communication is two-way in method but directed to benefit the organization more than the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners conduct research to craft persuasive messages and modify publics’ attitudes/behaviors; the interaction is not aimed primarily at mutual understanding but at influencing publics in the organization’s favor. Evaluation focuses on effectiveness of persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of practice: two-way symmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-way symmetric model: mutual understanding is the objective; PR adapts organization and environment to each other for the benefit of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model emphasizes negotiation, two-way dialogue, counseling management to change organizational behavior when needed, and seeking mutually satisfactory solutions. Considered the most 'advanced' model and linked to ethical/responsible practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR as an organizational subsystem and boundary role
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations functions as a subsystem (often part of management) that serves as a boundary liaison between the organization and external groups and between subsystems within the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR supports production, disposal (marketing/distribution), maintenance (personnel), adaptive (R&D/planning), and management subsystems. Boundary role: one foot inside organization, one outside; helps communicate across organizational boundaries and brings external ideas in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of effects and inclusivity of definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of PR should not be restricted to one desired effect (persuasion vs understanding); PR can aim at persuasion, mutual understanding, or simple communication; ineffective or irresponsible practice still falls under PR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns against narrowing the term to only ethical/successful practice. Examples: persuasion emphasized by some authors; mutual understanding by others. The working definition used intentionally includes professional and nonprofessional activities and various effects.
